records.section: Preparation of the next periodic report
records.text: 45. The Committee recommends that the State Party submit its combined twenty ‐ sixth to thirtieth periodic reports, as a single document, by 4 January 2030, taking into account the reporting guidelines adopted by the Committee during its seventy-first session and addressing all the points raised in the present concluding observations. In the light of General Assembly resolution 68/268, the Committee urges the State Party to observe the limit of 21,200 words for periodic reports.
themes: Cooperation & Follow up with Treaty Bodies

records.text: 44. In accordance with article 9 (1) of the Convention and rule 74 of its rules of procedure, the Committee requests the State Party to provide, within one year of the adoption of the present concluding observations, information on its implementation of the recommendations contained in paragraphs 16 (e) (awareness campaigns promoting tolerance and diversity), 18 (d) (awareness-raising among migrant workers) and 30 (language barriers) above.

records.text: 43. The Committee wishes to draw the attention of the State Party to the particular importance of the recommendations contained in paragraphs 10 (training on the Convention), 12 (comprehensive anti ‐discrimination legislation), 14 (strengthening the Commissioner for Administration and the Protection of Human Rights (Ombudsman)) and 35 (ratification of other treaties) above and requests the State Party to provide detailed information in its next periodic report on the concrete measures taken to implement those recommendations.

records.text: 42. The Committee encourages the State Party to update its common core document, which dates to 2018, in accordance with the harmonized guidelines on reporting under the international human rights treaties, in particular those on the common core document, as adopted at the fifth inter-committee meeting of the human rights treaty bodies, held in June 2006. In the light of General Assembly resolution 68/268, the Committee urges the State Party to observe the limit of 42,400 words for such documents.
themes: Cooperation & Follow up with Treaty Bodies

records.text: 41. The Committee recommends that the State Party’s reports be made readily available and accessible to the public at the time of their submission and that the concluding observations of the Committee with respect to those reports be similarly made available to all government bodies entrusted with the implementation of the Convention, in particular the national mechanism for implementation, reporting and follow-up, and publicized on the website of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in the official and other commonly used languages, as appropriate.

records.text: 40. The Committee recommends that the State Party continue consulting and increasing its dialogue with civil society organizations working in the area of human rights protection, in particular those working to combat racial discrimination, in connection with the preparation of the next periodic report and in follow-up to the present concluding observations.

records.section: International Decade for People of African Descent
records.text: 39. In its resolution 79/193, the General Assembly proclaimed 2025–2034 the Second International Decade for People of African Descent. Also in that resolution, the Assembly decided to extend the programme of activities for the implementation of the International Decade for People of African Descent adopted in its resolution 69/16, with a view to ensuring continuing efforts in promoting the respect, protection and fulfilment of all human rights and fundamental freedoms of people of African descent. In the light of this development, the Committee recommends that the State Party implement the programme of activities in collaboration with people of African descent and include in its next periodic report information on the measures adopted in that framework, taking into account the Committee’s general recommendation No. 34 (2011) on racial discrimination against people of African descent.
themes: Cooperation & Follow up with Treaty Bodies

records.section: Follow-up to the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action
records.text: 38. In the light of its general recommendation No. 33 (2009) on follow-up to the Durban Review Conference, the Committee recommends that , when implementing the Convention in its domestic legal order, the State Party give effect to the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, adopted in September 2001 by the World Conference against Racism, Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and Related Intolerance, taking into account the outcome document of the Durban Review Conference, held in Geneva in April 2009 . The Committee requests that the State Party include in its next periodic report specific information on action plans and other measures taken to implement the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action at the national level.

records.text: 34. The Committee recommends that the State Party: (a) Adopt and effectively implement comprehensive anti-racism policies and programmes in the education sector, including awareness-raising, teacher training and age-appropriate curricula addressing racial discrimination; (b) Ensure that all incidents of racist bullying and violence are systematically recorded, investigated and sanctioned and that victims have access to effective reporting mechanisms and support services; (c) Strengthen the mandate and capacity of the Observatory on School Violence, including by collecting and publishing disaggregated statistics on incidents of school violence, including, where appropriate and in line with human rights standards on data protection, information on the ethnic origin of victims; (d) Engage with affected communities, including people of African descent, in the design and evaluation of policies aimed at combating racial discrimination in schools.

records.text: 32. The Committee, recalling its general recommendation No. 27 (2000) on discrimination against Roma, recommends that the State Party recognize Roma (Kurbet) as a distinct ethnic minority. It reiterates its previous recommendation that the State Party step up efforts to address the precarious situation of the Roma (Kurbet) community and calls upon the State Party to ensure that measures taken, including through the National Roma Strategic Framework (2021–2030), secure their integration and address the stigmatization, marginalization and racial discrimination that they experience. It requests the State Party to provide information on measures taken and progress made in its next periodic report.

records.text: 31. The Committee notes the information provided by the State Party regarding the National Roma Strategic Framework (2021–2030). However, the Committee is concerned that the State Party considers Roma (Kurbet) as part of the Turkish Cypriot community, and not as a distinct ethnic minority. The Committee remains concerned that Roma (Kurbet) continue to experience discrimination, including in employment, poorer living conditions and general stigmatization, and face difficulties in access to adequate housing, water, electricity and sanitation, exposure to racist speech and attacks and difficulties in access to education, with Roma (Kurbet) children experiencing low school attendance and high dropout rates (arts. 2 and 5).

records.text: 30. The Committee recommends that the State Party eliminate discriminatory language barriers and ensure the effective use of Turkish in public administration and education.

29. Noting the information provided by the State Party regarding measures to expand the teaching and use of the Turkish language, the Committee is concerned about reports that language requirements for certain types of jobs, including Greek language proficiency tests, may have a discriminatory effect in practice, despite Turkish being an official language of the State Party. The Committee is also concerned about reports of the limited use in practice of the Turkish language in public administration and education, including the insufficient availability of Turkish-language education in certain areas (arts. 2 and 5).
sdg_targets: 4.a: Build and upgrade inclusive and safe schools

records.text: 28. The Committee recommends that the State Party take concrete and targeted measures to eliminate structural barriers affecting Turkish Cypriots, including by ensuring non-discriminatory access to nationality in practice, promoting effective representation in public institutions and guaranteeing equal access in practice to public services, employment, healthcare and cultural and social life, in line with the Constitution of the State Party. It also recommends that the State Party monitor implementation and provide information on progress achieved.
sdg_targets: 3.8: Achieve universal health coverage

records.text: 27. The Committee is concerned about reports of obstacles faced by Turkish Cypriots in the equal enjoyment of rights, including as set out in the Constitution of the State Party, compared to Greek Cypriots, including for children of mixed marriages involving Turkish Cypriots, who reportedly face significant difficulties in acquiring nationality. The Committee is also concerned about reports of the limited integration of Turkish Cypriots into public institutions, including the civil service, the police and the judiciary. It is further concerned about reports of unequal access to services and opportunities, including in healthcare, employment, public broadcasting and participation in sports and cultural life (arts. 2 and 5).
sdg_targets: 16.3: Promote the rule of law and access to justice for all

records.section: Intercommunal initiatives, interaction and freedom of movement
records.text: 26. The Committee recommends that the State Party expand and strengthen measures to promote sustained intercommunal engagement, including by increasing the number of crossing points and removing the legal, practical and administrative barriers under its control to facilitate the freedom of movement of both communities.

records.section: Intercommunal initiatives, interaction and freedom of movement
records.text: 25. While the Committee notes the information provided by the State Party regarding measures to promote intercommunal contact and cooperation between the Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot communities, it is concerned about reports indicating that such initiatives remain limited in scope and impact. The Committee is also concerned about obstacles affecting freedom of movement, including legal, administrative and practical barriers, which may hinder meaningful interaction between the communities. The Committee is further concerned about the lack of detailed information on measures taken to facilitate sustained intercommunal engagement (arts. 2 and 5).

24. The Committee recommends that the State Party: (a) Ensure the full and effective enforcement of the law on the prevention and combating of trafficking in and exploitation of persons and the protection of victims of 2014 and subsequent amendments, and allocate adequate resources for its implementation; (b) Strengthen mechanisms for the early identification of victims of trafficking, including among migrant workers, and provide victims with immediate protection and assistance; (c) Continue and intensify efforts to investigate, prosecute and convict perpetrators of trafficking, ensuring that penalties are commensurate with the gravity of the crime, and refrain from deporting victims of trafficking; (d) Enhance mechanisms to identify victims of trafficking in persons, including reviewing deficiencies in the identification of persons subjected to trafficking for purposes of labour exploitation, in particular in agriculture and construction.
themes: Human trafficking & contemporary forms of slavery
sdg_targets: 8.8: Universal labour rights and safe working environments
8.7: End modern slavery, trafficking and child labour

records.text: 23. The Committee acknowledges the range of measures taken by the State Party to prevent trafficking in persons, to protect and support victims and to strengthen the prosecution of perpetrators, including through the 2019 amendment to the law on the prevention and combating of trafficking in and exploitation of persons and the protection of victims of 2014 (Act No. 60(I)/2014), which criminalizes receiving services from a victim of trafficking in persons. The Committee also acknowledges the increase in the number of convictions for trafficking. However, the Committee is concerned that trafficking in persons for the purposes of labour and sexual exploitation remains a problem in the State Party, particularly affecting migrant women from Asia, Eastern Europe and sub-Saharan Africa, and that victims of trafficking are sometimes deported (arts. 2, 5 and 6).

records.section: Rights of refugees, asylum-seekers and stateless persons
records.text: 22. Recalling its general recommendation No. 30 (2004) on discrimination against non-citizens, the Committee recommends that the State Party: (a) Expand and strengthen measures to ensure adequate conditions and capacity in reception centres; (b) Expedite the identification of vulnerable persons and guarantee effective access for refugees, asylum-seekers and stateless persons to essential services, including healthcare, housing, education and employment, without discrimination; (c) Ensure respect for the right to seek asylum by enabling effective access to its territory and complying fully with the principle of non-refoulement; (d) Take effective measures to prevent statelessness, ensuring that all children born in the State Party, including children of undocumented migrant workers, asylum ‐ seekers and stateless persons, are registered at birth without discrimination.

records.section: Rights of refugees, asylum-seekers and stateless persons
records.text: 21. The Committee notes the information provided by the State Party regarding receiving and assisting a significant number of asylum-seekers and refugees. However, it is concerned about reports indicating challenges in ensuring the full enjoyment of rights by refugees, asylum-seekers and stateless persons without discrimination. In particular, it is concerned about inadequate reception conditions and capacity, delays in the identification of vulnerable persons and barriers in access to essential services, including healthcare, housing, education and employment (arts. 2 and 5).
sdg_targets: 11.1: Safe and affordable housing

records.text: 20. The Committee recommends that the State Party: (a) Ensure that the detention of migrants is used only as a measure of last resort, for the shortest possible period and subject to judicial oversight; (b) Ensure that all operations aimed at identifying undocumented migrants comply fully with international human rights standards and guarantee that no migrant is detained or deported without due process, including prompt judicial review of detention; (c) Guarantee that all migrants, including undocumented migrants, have access to legal aid, interpretation services and information on their rights in a language that they understand; (d) Enhance measures to prevent the abuse of migrants in detention, including by strengthening independent monitoring and complaint mechanisms; (e) Ensure that the conditions in detention centres are reviewed and improved so that essential services, including access to healthcare and education for children, are in full compliance with international humanitarian standards; (f) Collect and regularly publish disaggregated statistics on the prosecution and detention of non-citizens, including migrant workers.

records.text: 19. Noting the information provided by the State Party regarding institutional reforms, improved detention standards and training programmes for relevant staff, the Committee is concerned about reports of the continued use of detention of migrants, including for the purpose of deportation, reportedly as a routine measure and for prolonged periods. The Committee is also concerned about reports that migrants awaiting deportation are in some cases detained together with persons charged with criminal offences. It is further concerned about inadequate reception conditions and capacity, including reports that not all asylum‐seekers undergo vulnerability assessments, that they may remain for extended periods in reception facilities and that conditions in such facilities are in certain cases substandard (arts. 2 and 5).
affected_persons: Persons deprived of their liberty & detainees

records.text: 18. The Committee recommends that the State Party: (a) Review its migration and labour policies with a view to repealing dependency on a single employer, including by enabling migrant workers to change employers and sever ties with recruitment agencies without jeopardizing their residence status; (b) Strengthen labour inspections and enforcement mechanisms, including in sectors with a high risk of exploitation and occupational hazards, such as agriculture, domestic work and the service industry, and ensure that all allegations of abuse are promptly, effectively and impartially investigated, that perpetrators are prosecuted and that the sanctions imposed are commensurate with the offence; (c) Prevent and effectively sanction the confiscation of identity documents by employers, ensure the timely and full payment of wages and improve oversight of the working and living conditions of migrant workers, including domestic workers working in private households; (d) Increase awareness among migrant workers of their rights, including through targeted outreach and information campaigns in relevant languages.

records.text: 17. The Committee is concerned about reports of exploitation and abuse of migrant workers in the State Party, including those employed in low-skilled sectors such as agriculture, domestic work and services. It is also concerned about allegations of excessive working hours, non-payment or delayed payment of wages, confiscation of identity documents and substandard living conditions. The Committee is further concerned that migrant workers’ residence status often continues to be tied to a specific employer, which may create dependency and increase their vulnerability to abuse. The Committee is concerned about reports of barriers faced by migrant workers in accessing justice and effective remedies, including limited access to legal aid, fear of retaliation or deportation, language barriers and insufficient labour inspections, particularly in private households employing domestic workers (arts. 2 and 5).

records.text: 16. Recalling its general recommendation No. 35 (2013) on combating racist hate speech, the Committee recommends that the State Party: (a) Take comprehensive measures to monitor and address hate speech in traditional media, on the Internet, on social media platforms and at sports events, including by establishing effective mechanisms for reporting and removing racist content online; (b) Continue to collect and publish disaggregated statistics on hate speech and hate crimes as separate categories of crimes, including the number of complaints, investigations, prosecutions and convictions, and provide this information in its next periodic report; (c) Intensify training for law enforcement officials, prosecutors and judges on identifying, investigating and prosecuting hate speech and hate crimes, and ensure that victims have access to effective remedies; (d) Develop and implement strategies to combat xenophobia and negative stereotypes against Turkish Cypriots, as well as Muslim communities, people of African descent and non-citizens, including migrant workers and others considered as such; (e) Expand public awareness campaigns promoting tolerance and diversity and ensure that political discourse does not incite racial hatred or discrimination.

records.text: 15. The Committee notes the various legislative and policy measures enacted by the State Party to prevent and combat hate speech, including improved hate crime recording mechanisms and guidance, expanded training programmes for police and the AWARE campaign. However, the Committee is concerned about: (a) Inadequate measures to monitor and address hate speech in the media, on the Internet, on social media platforms and in connection with sports events; (b) The lack of distinction between hate speech and hate crimes in public records; (c) Reports of xenophobic expressions against Turkish Cypriots, non-citizens, particularly migrant workers, Muslim communities and persons of African descent, who are frequently portrayed as threats to employment, the demographic composition of the population, culture or religion, and the use of xenophobia as a political tool, including by Members of Parliament; (d) Inadequate implementation of the European Union regulatory framework on digital services pertaining to initiatives to address illegal hate speech online (arts. 1, 4 and 6).

records.text: 13. While welcoming the accreditation with A status of the Office of the Commissioner for Administration and the Protection of Human Rights (Ombudsman), and the measures adopted to strengthen it, including the increase in staff in recent years, the Committee is concerned that the human, technical and financial resources allocated to the Commission remain insufficient for it to effectively execute its mandate, including pertaining to the volume of cases related to racial discrimination. It is also concerned that complaints of racial discrimination are not clearly analysed and disaggregated by specific grounds of discrimination, which limits the ability to identify and demonstrate qualitative and quantitative trends (art. 2).

records.text: 12. The Committee recommends that the State Party adopt comprehensive anti ‐discrimination legislation containing an explicit definition of racial discrimination on all the grounds enumerated in article 1 of the Convention and expressly prohibiting structural, direct, indirect and intersecting forms of discrimination in both the public and the private spheres. The Committee invites the State Party to make full use of the Convention and the Committee’s general recommendations when preparing such legislation.

records.text: 11. The Committee notes the information provided by the State Party regarding the protection against racial discrimination afforded by the Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities and the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages – to both of which Cyprus is a Party – as well as article 28 of the Constitution, guaranteeing equality before the law and prohibiting discrimination, including on the grounds of race, community, religion, language and ethnic or social origin. However, the Committee is concerned that the absence of a unified anti-discrimination law fully reflecting the scope of the Convention may leave gaps in the State Party’s ability to adequately address racial discrimination (arts. 1, 2 and 6).

records.text: 10. The Committee recommends that the State Party conduct training programmes and awareness-raising campaigns, in particular for judges, prosecutors, lawyers, law enforcement officials and other relevant civil servants, to ensure that the provisions of the Convention are invoked, when relevant, by and before domestic courts. It requests the State Party to include in its next periodic report specific examples of the application of the Convention by all levels of domestic courts.

records.text: 9. The Committee notes the information provided by the State Party that ratified international treatiesare part of the domestic legal order pursuant to the Constitution. The Committee nevertheless regrets the limited information provided on cases in which the provisions of the Convention were invoked before or applied by domestic courts, including lower-level courts (art. 2).

records.text: 8. Recalling its previous recommendation and its general recommendations No. 4 (1973) concerning reporting by States Parties under article 1 of the Convention, No. 8 (1990) concerning the interpretation and application of article 1 (1) and (4) of the Convention and No. 24 (1999) concerning article 1 of the Convention, the Committee recommends that the State Party: (a) Include, in its next periodic report, reliable, up-to-date and comprehensive statistics on the demographic and ethnic composition of the population, based on the principle of self-identification, including detailed statistics on ethnic groups and non-citizens such as migrants, refugees, asylum-seekers and stateless persons; (b) Produce updated disaggregated statistics on the socioeconomic situation of ethnic groups and non-citizens, including on their access to education, employment, healthcare and housing, with a view to creating a detailed empirical basis for assessing the equal enjoyment of the rights enshrined in the Convention.

records.text: 6. The Committee encourages the State Party to continue its engagement in the peace process in order to seek a comprehensive settlement to the problem. In addition, the Committee continues to support the recommendations of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights with regard to addressing underlying human rights concerns, in particular with regard to rights also enshrined in the Convention. The Committee requests the State Party to continue to provide it with updated information on efforts to improve relations between the two communities.

5. The Committee welcomes the ongoing peace process. The Committee is aware that the protracted conflict in Cyprus and the continued division of the island contributes to the ongoing tensions between the Greek Cypriot and the Turkish Cypriot communities.

4. While the Committee notes that the State Party does not exercise effective control over all of its territory and is thus unable to ensure the full application of the Convention, it remains concerned that the current political situation hinders efforts to protect vulnerable groups covered by the Convention in the territory under its control.

3. The Committee welcomes the following legislative, institutional and policy measures taken by the State Party: (a) The amendment in 2017 of the Criminal Code to explicitly allow courts to consider racist and xenophobic motivation as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing; (b) The enactment in 2018 of Act No. 73(I)/2018) establishing the Administrative Court of International Protection, aimed at improving access to justice and expediting asylum-related cases; (c) Amendments in 2016 to the legal aid law extending access to legal aid for applicants for international protection, including judicial review of asylum-related decisions; (d) The measures taken in 2019 to strengthen the Office of the Ombudsperson, including the approval of additional staff posts and reforms to the recruitment procedure; (e) The adoption in 2021 of the first national strategy for the protection and promotion of human rights; (f) The institutionalization and yearly monitoring of the Code of Conduct against Racism and Guide for Managing and Recording Racist Incidents (first introduced in 2014).

records.text: 74. With regard to private security companies in the maritime context, the Working Group recommends that the Republic of Cyprus: (a) Adopt a comprehensive governance strategy that connects maritime and labour-related authorities, including port operators, customs officials, inspectors, law enforcement officials, shipowners, ship agents, crew managers, private security companies and other stakeholders to enhance coordination, joint operations, inter ‐ agency enforcement and data-sharing; (b) Ensure effective monitoring, oversight and enforcement capacity, with sufficient budgeting and staffing to carry out systematic and unannounced regular vessel inspections before entering and existing high-risk areas within territorial seas, to ensure adequate storage of arms on vessels and ensure that the deployment of unarmed and armed private security personnel comply with international human rights and labour standards; (c) Ensure that private military and security companies adopt clear policies and procedures regarding the use of force at sea, the management, transfer and possession of appropriate storage containers for weapons and ammunition, especially in the context of floating armouries, the vetting and regular training of personnel, including on human rights, labour standards and trauma-informed approaches, and ensuring the adoption of human rights-compatible corporate-level mechanisms; (d) Ensure that all persons on board ships are informed of their human rights and have access to multilingual complaint mechanisms, including anonymous reporting tools, legal support and referral pathways in the case of violations; (e) Carry out effective, impartial and timely investigations into every allegation of the unlawful use of force or other violations, impose commensurate punishments and provide guarantees of non-repetition; (f) Restrict the use of force and firearms in compliance with international principles, particularly the principles of legality, precaution, necessity, proportionality, accountability and non-discrimination, and take steps to effectively protect the rights to life and security of persons; (g) Consider mutual cooperation in order to facilitate investigations and prosecution, including through legal assistance and extradition agreements, to ensure effective remedies; (h) Continue implementing standards developed by multi-stakeholder initiatives on the provision of private military and security at sea, such as the reference document of the Montreux Document Forum Working Group on the use of private military and security companies in maritime security entitled “ Elements for a maritime interpretation of the Montreux Document ” , in which the Group sets out good practices relating to the hiring of maritime private military and security companies; (i) Take the steps necessary to ensure that the private military and security companies authorized to operate at sea are certified members of the International Code of Conduct for Private Security Service Providers ’ Association and/or are certified to ISO standard 28007-1:2015. 75. In the light of the findings detailed in the present report, the Working Group recommends that the Republic of Cyprus and the international community develop binding international regulations to regulate the use of unarmed and armed security personnel in land-based and maritime operations, in line with international human rights standards.

records.text: 73. With regard to private military and security companies, the Working Group recommends that the Republic of Cyprus: (a) Notwithstanding the existing police oversight mechanism, consider establishing an operational long-term, sustainable and adequately funded independent mechanism, with sufficient staffing and resources, to strengthen coordination, monitoring, inspection and oversight of private security companies and personnel to ensure compliance and enforcement across the country and abroad; (b) Ensure mandatory ongoing training and the continuous professional development of private security personnel by private security companies, including on human rights, the use of force, de-escalation protocols, respect for cultural diversity, intercultural communication and protection from sexual exploitation and abuse; (c) Consider adopting measures to ensure the increased harmonization and standardization of content between the training provided by recognized trainers and institutions, as well as by private security companies, for continuous training and refresher courses; (d) Strengthen preventive strategies and ensure that international human rights standards are incorporated into the training manuals and internal ethics policies of private security companies and that such standards become a standard requirement for licensing; (e) Ensure that the criteria and qualifications for recognized trainers and institutions are robust and that regular ongoing assessment is conducted to ensure that high-quality and human rights-based training is provided to security personnel; (f) Ensure that private security personnel do not perform functions that are the responsibility of the State security apparatus; (g) Ensure that contracts between public agencies and private military and security companies include sufficiently detailed obligations with regard to international human rights standards and that they establish a clear delineation of responsibilities, including reporting requirements, and effective means for addressing contractor non ‐ compliance, including contract termination and civil and criminal liability; (h) Strengthen measures to ensure the accountability of companies and their personnel operating in and from the Republic of Cyprus for human rights violations and abuses caused directly or indirectly by their business activities. This should include raising the awareness of members of the public of regulatory protections and establishing grievance and compliant mechanism, with standardized methods for reporting on and reviewing use of force by security personnel to ensure investigation, prosecution, extraterritorial application and punishment of companies and personnel, and measures to ensure non-repetition; (i) Ensure that companies exercise heightened human rights due diligence to avoid causing, contributing or becoming directly linked to adverse human rights impacts. This due diligence process should take place at all stages of their operations in order to capture potential and actual human rights impacts, in line with the Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights; (j) Ensure that, where companies identify that they have caused or contributed to adverse human rights impacts, such companies should fully disclose information pertaining to those impacts and provide or cooperate in their remediation through legitimate processes. In instances in which those impacts amount to human rights violations and abuses, including crimes, they should fully cooperate with judicial mechanisms leading to accountability and effective remedies for victims; (k) Consider participating in the sessions of the open-ended intergovernmental working group to elaborate the content of an international regulatory framework on the regulation, monitoring and oversight of the activities of private military and security companies; (l) Join the International Code of Conduct for Private Security Service Providers ’ Association, the Voluntary Principles on Security and Human Rights and the Montreux Document Forum in support of good practices and the effective regulation of private military and security companies.

records.text: 68. The Republic of Cyprus has made notable strides towards regulating and strengthening standards governing private security companies within the maritime sector, in line with international standards. Its stringent registration requirements and commitment to safety, security and compliance in the use of unarmed and armed security personnel on its flag State vessels in high-risk areas at sea is commendable. High standards and compliance are critical in ensuring protection against human rights abuses or criminal activities, especially given that arms and use of force can be used in these contexts. 69. While recognizing the positive steps that have been taken by the Republic of Cyprus to regulate private security companies in the maritime context, the same high standards and scrutiny need to be applied to those operating on land. With such a high number of private security personnel in the country, the Working Group highlights the need to establish an independent and proper oversight body or mechanism to effectively oversee them and to ensure that private security actors are not engaged in human rights abuses. The new amendments to the law on private security companies will provide an opportunity for human rights standards to be incorporated. 70. The Working Group stands ready to cooperate with the Republic of Cyprus as well as the private security industry, both maritime and land-based, to ensure that the delivery of private security services respects the full range of human rights of those it serves.

records.section: Domestic regulation of private security companies operating at sea
records.text: 47. In 2012, Law 77(I)/2012 on the Protection of Cyprus Ships Against Acts of Piracy and Other Unlawful Acts was adopted, with oversight by the Shipping Deputy Ministry, to enhance the security of ships bearing the flag of the Republic of Cyprus while at sea. It requires flag State vessels to implement compulsory security measures and precautions when navigating through high-risk areas, in addition to provisions of chapter XI-2 of the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, 1974, and the International Code for the Security of Ships and of Port Facilities to ensure and maintain the security of the ship and prevent all forms of unlawful actsor attempts to violate the security of the ship. 48. Law 77(I)/2012 also establishes a legislative framework for the use of privately contracted unarmed and armed security personnel on board flag State vessels when sailing through high-riskareas such as the north-west Indian Ocean, the Arabian Sea, the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. The Shipping Deputy Ministry, on the basis of a reasoned and justified security risk assessment, is responsible for the authorization for the engagement of the services of a private security company for a particular voyage. 49. Under Law 77(I)/2012, private security companies must be vetted and certified by the Shipping Deputy Ministry before providing security-related services on flag State vessels. The law also lays out stringent requirements and conditions regarding the registration and determination of services, the types of equipment and weapons permitted and the issuing, suspension and cancellation of licences and certificates. From 2022 to 2024, the number of approved passages through high-risk areas for which private security services were permitted reduced by 80 per cent (from about 231 to 49). Officials informed the delegation that the reason for that was that companies were using alternative, safer passages at sea or usingOperation ASPIDES of the European Union Naval Forceinstead of hiring unarmed and armed guards on vessels. 50. In 2017, the Shipping Deputy Ministry issued circular No. 9/2017, providing detailed instructions and guidelines applicable to private security companies, namely: (a) general instructions; (b) information on firearms (containing information on, inter alia, the categories of permitted firearms and the requirements for export licences and/or end user certificates); and (c) guidance on the documentation to be submitted with the application for the issue of the certificate (including the content of the standard operating procedures that are required to be developed by each private security company). Furthermore, the Shipping Deputy Ministry issued circular No. 26/2017, which limits the ratio between security personnel and firearms. For each approved private security personnel, the private security company can register up to two firearms on its certificate issued by the Republic of Cyprus. 51. In 2023 and 2024, the Shipping Deputy Ministry produced additional orders, temporary measures and circulars (circulars No. 30/2023, No. 6/2024, No. 14/2024 and No.28/2024) to provide guidance to flag State vessels in response to the situation in the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. The guidance emerged as a response to the reported continuation of attacks by Houthi forces against ships crossing the Bab-al-Mandab strait and extending the high-risk areas to cover areas of guerrilla attacks. The Working Group sees value in adding human rights principles into the various circulars and guidance documents, especially when such personnel are armed and can use force. 52. During the visit, the delegation was informed that the following 12 private security companies held a certificate (valid for two years) with Republic of Cyprus: (a) Ambrey; (b) Interarma; (c) Diaplous; (d) ESC Global Security; (e) Forte Maritime Security; (f) LSS (Cyprus); (g) Maritime Defence Force; (h) Open Ocean Services; (i) Premium Focus Nautilus Maritime Security Services; (j) Sea Guardian; (k) Triaena Maritime Security Ltd.; and (l) United Guards Services Ltd. The delegation met with representatives of some of those companies and was impressed with the level of assessment, vetting, due diligence checks and compliance that were required in order to receive certification. The delegation was informed that the deployment of unarmed and armed security personnel on flag State vessels had been satisfactory and that their use across high-risk areas had contributed to a substantial reduction in piracy-related and other unlawful attacks. 53. Since 2012, there has been a noticeable reduction in the number of certificates issued to private security companies. The delegation was informed that approximately 60 companies had been removed from the list of approved companies by the Shipping Deputy Ministry as a result of: (a) expiration of certificate; (b) winding down or ceasing of operations; or (c) one year having elapsed without providing any services on board a ship. Through its network of authorized inspectors, the Shipping Deputy Ministry conducts inspections of vessels before registration. The Working Group sees value in regular inspections before, during and after registration and voyages to ensure that the personnel on board and the inventory carried match all documented declarations, that firearms, ammunition and security equipment are stored appropriately and that there are no human rights and labour issues of concern. 54. In line with circular No. 9/2017, private security companies must include the following information in their standard operating procedures when submitting them for approval to the Shipping Deputy Ministry: the procedures in place for checking the security personnel’s qualifications and minimum military service requirements (such as age, service time and training); procedures to ensure understanding of applicable laws and intended activities when carrying out training programmes for security personnel, including a full schedule showing the themes and the duration of each training session; the briefing given to security personnel on the mission, the risk assessment and the specificities of the voyage (e.g. type of ship, cargo and crew) prior to boarding; and mandatory performance evaluation of their security personnel. 55. Nevertheless, the Working Group sees value in putting in place compulsory prerequisites and oversight mechanisms to attest to and oversee the hiring and training process of security personnel in order to ensure that certain minimum requirements are met by entities and to determine the suitability of security personnel to be deployed to prevent human rights violations in that context. The Working Group considers that measures should be taken to strengthen the training undertaken by security personnel, particularly by ensuring comprehensive, wide-ranging and regular training on the following themes: (a) knowledge of maritime security procedures and shipboard familiarization, including communication protocols and understanding of chain of command; (b) international human rights, labour and humanitarian standards, including use of force; (c) weapons and ammunition storage and management, including floating armouries; (d) hostile environment training, de-escalation and response plans; (e) medical and psychological training, including trauma-based approaches; (f) respect for cultural diversity; (g) prevention of sexual abuse and exploitation; (h) recording and reporting of incidents; and (i) interacting with relevant authorities and law enforcement entities. 56. Concerning the use of force, private security companies must have in place a procedure on the rules of engagement of their security personnel, covering all levels of escalation. The rules on use of force must clearly state that: (a) no firearms are to be deployed by private security personnel unless authorized by the master of the ship; and (b) only the master of the ship will liaise with the on-board team with regard to any instructions, decisions, permission or authorization needed on the implementation of the provisions of the law and arrangements as necessary for immediate response to any alerts from the guards on board (unless the master delegates this to any other officer). The circumstances for the use of force should be documented and its use is subject to the prior authorization of the master of the ship. The Working Group notes the need to clearly define and limit the use of force in compliance with international principles on the use of force and firearms, particularly the principles of legality, precaution, necessity, proportionality, accountability and non‐discrimination. 57. With regard to weapons management, Law 77(I)/2012 stipulates that the master of the ship has the obligation to supervise, monitor and control the storage, transportation and unloading of weapons and equipment from the ship. The storage of weapons and equipment on the ship should be done in such a way as to ensure that persons on board the ship would not have access to them. The private security company should only have access to them when in high-risk areas and when their use is necessary, and in connection with their unloading from the ship. 58. The use of weapons by security personnel is not allowed in internal or territorial waters, except if the competent authorities have allowed it or it is set out in the terms and conditions of the certificates issued. No other person on board is permitted to use the firearms and security equipment carried on board. The Republic of Cyprus prohibits the loading onto and unloading from a ship, firearms and security equipment for use by private security companies within internal waters, territorial sea or in contiguous zone. However, it is permitted for security personnel to embark and disembark from a vessel or craft on the high seas, irrespective of the flag it is entitled to fly, as well as load, unload and transfer firearms and security equipment. 59. The master of the ship and the ship operator have the obligation to immediately report to the Shipping Deputy Ministry an unlawful act or an attempt to commit an unlawful act and whenever use is made of the firearms and security equipment carried on board. As a general rule, the master of the ship and each member of the crew may arrest, search, imprison, confiscate and detain any person found on board who has committed, is committing or attempts to commit an unlawful act against the ship or the persons on board or the cargo transported, when on the high seas or the territorial sea. 60. In addition, the master of the ship also has the following obligations: (a) to immediately report to the Shipping Deputy Ministry any arrest, search, detention, seizure, impoundment or custody; (b) to supervise and monitor the imprisonment and guarding on board, the transfer from and the disembarkation from the ship of any person who has been arrested and/or imprisoned; and (c) to ensure satisfactory accommodation, food, healthcare and security for any person who has been arrested and/or imprisoned until disembarkation from the ship. 61. Officials informed the delegation that there had been no complaints by any seafarer, guard or other person with regard to services provided by private security companies on board flag State vessels or for any other matter falling under the legislation. There had been no reported cases of firearms being used or engaged. The delegation received no information about complaints, arrests or prosecutions relating to human rights violations perpetrated by armed guards operating on flag State or commercial vessels. 62. An important specific phenomenon concerning the proliferation of weapons at sea is the emergence of floating armouries, by which some private military and security companies have resorted to the storing of firearms and accommodation of personnel in international waters in separate vessels or crafts. This approach allows security personnel to embark on client ships without weapons, obtaining them later once the ships are outside internal, territorial or contiguous waters. The Working Group has voiced serious concern regarding this practice, in particular in terms of weapons diversion, as these floating armouries operate in a legal grey area, without clear international, regional or national regulations governing their operation, management and transport and the use of weapons. 63. According to the authorities of the Republic of Cyprus, firearms kept in controlled floating armouries are only loaded onto the flag State vessel at the start of its passage through a high-risk area. During the passage, the firearms are kept locked by the captain and are only provided to security personnel if there is an imminent threat. The firearms are subsequently unloaded back on to floating armouries at the end of the passage. This phenomenon highlights the importance of strengthening and adopting clear policies and procedures on the management, transfer, storage and use of firearms and other weapons, especially in the context of floating armouries, as there are no verifications or controls once on the high seas. 64. In cases of contravention or suspected contravention of Law 77(I)/2012, the penalties provided for include the suspension and cancellation (withdrawal) of certificates issued by the Shipping Deputy Ministry to private security companies or operators of flag ship vessels; the imposition of a fine by the Shipping Deputy Ministry not exceeding €50,000 and/or; imprisonment for a term not exceeding 15 years or a fine not exceeding €75,000; or both sanctions. The delegation was informed that administrative fines had been imposed on private security companies and ship operators on about six occasions in the previous 10 years on the grounds of: (a) not informing the Shipping Deputy Ministry of changes within the company or a change of director; or (b) the boarding of security personnel prior to the issuing of the ship’scertificate for the passage. Officials also informed the delegation of reported incidents that did not relate to the engagement and deployment of firearms, such as an incident involving a fight between two armed guards on a ship, a suspected skiff approaching a ship and two missiles being launched and then exploding near a ship. 65. Worldwide, in general, the operation of private security companies and their personnel in the maritime context can often give rise to certain specificities concerning violations of labour standards (e.g. rest periods, fair wages and living conditions) and threats to health and safety, including physical, psychological and social factors. High levels of stress and fatigue result in high levels of work-related accidents, injuries and diseases. The delegation was informed that migrant workers were often more vulnerable to different forms of exploitation, including low wages and minimal training. The incorporation of the Maritime Labour Convention, 2006, into the legal framework of the Republic of Cyprus entailed the establishment of procedures for the submission of seafarers’ complaints regarding breaches of their rights, and the fair and prompt handling of such complaints. The Shipping Deputy Ministry has in place two International Organization for Standardizationprocedures for handling seafarers’ on-board and onshore complaints. 66. Seafarers employed on flag State vessels navigating or operating in high-risk areas are entitled to exercise additional rights. Law 77(I)/2012 provides for: (a) an obligation not to abandon members of a ship’s personnel; (b) suspension of the right to terminate contracts of employment; (c) extension of the validity of contracts of employment; (d) obligation of the shipowner for payment of what has been agreed under the contract of employment; (e) entitlement to repatriation; (f) right to return to the ship; (g) compensation for illness or bodily injury; (h) compensation for injury or bodily injury by firearm or special security equipment; (i) mandatory medical examination upon termination of the unlawful possession of the ship; (j) medical care and maintenance; (k) the obligations of the master of the ship or the shipowner with regard to members of the ship personnel who are dead or missing; and (l) resolution of labour disputes. The delegation did not receive information indicating that seafarers had been abandoned or subjected to abuses by the personnel of private security companies. 67. Nonetheless, the Working Group highlights the need to ensure that adequate complaint and grievance mechanisms are in place to strengthen accountability and access to justice for potential human rights abuses occurring in the maritime context where private security company personnel operate. During the visit, it became evident that there is no independent body or mechanism to which an individual can report labour issues or human right abuses. There was limited information in the public domain or consideration of this specific aspect, and much reliance is placed on internal channels and processes. It was hard to determine which relevant authorities, entities and/or persons were responsible for providing assistance to seafarers, guards or any other person onboard with regard to complaints, investigations and pathways to referrals. The lack of attention, reporting and feasible information highlights the urgent need for greater action and awareness on this issue. It is unclear which competent authorities are responsible and hold jurisdiction to investigate crimes perpetrated. Precise numbers are unclear because of underreporting and the difficulty of overseeing working conditions is substantially reduced at sea without independent mechanisms. Overall, the combination of national legislation and international standards to regulate the use of private security companies within the maritime sector is quite exemplary. The Working Group was informed that Law 77(I)/2012 has been a model law for other flag States. Therefore, the Working Group hopes that the high standards in place for the use of private security companies within the maritime context will continue to be upheld. As such, it sees the need for consistent follow-up to ensure greater training, vetting and oversight and to ensure that all actors on flag State vessels operate in alignment with international human rights standards.

records.section: Context within the Republic of Cyprus
records.text: 43. The Republic of Cyprus is one of the main maritime powers of the world, with the eleventh largest merchant fleet globally and the third largest fleet in Europe. It is recognized as a high-quality and reputable flag in the maritime industry, with a high ranking in the Paris Memorandum of Understanding on Port State Control whitelist. Approximately 5 per cent of the world’s merchant fleet is managed by the Republic of Cyprus and more than 20 percent of global third-party ship management activity is undertaken by companies based in the country. It is home to more than 200 shipping companies that own, manage or operate over 2,500 ocean-going vessels, totalling 91 million gross tons. The shipping industry has played a decisive role in the political, economic and social development of the Republic of Cyprus, representing 7 per cent of the country’s GDP (amounting to approximately €1.2billion). The industry provides 9,000 job opportunities onshore and more than 80,000 seafarers of various nationalities are employed on flag ship vessels. 44. Given its strong maritime culture and strategic geographical position, the Republic of Cyprus has played a prominent role in forming global maritime policies, with a strong presence in maritime affairs and shipping forums, including IMO, the International Labour Organization and the European Union. It has been a member of IMO since 1973 and has been elected to the IMO Council biennially since 1987. It has also provided much-needed support to enhance the capabilities of States through multilateral collaboration and technical cooperation. This includes providing specialized training for law enforcement officers at the newly established Cyprus Centre for Land, Open Seas and Port Security in Larnaca, with the support of the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime through its Global Maritime Crime Programme. 45. Moreover, the Republic of Cyprus has ratified all the main international instruments dealing with maritime issues and is a party to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, the Convention for the Suppression of Unlawful Acts against the Safety of Maritime Navigation and the Protocols thereto, the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime, the Maritime Labour Convention, 2006, the International Convention on Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping for Seafarers, 1978 the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, 1974, and the International Convention against the Taking of Hostages. 46. The Working Group recognizes that the reference document developed by the Maritime Working Group of the Montreux Document Forum constitutes key guidance to assist States in regulating the private military and security industry in maritime contexts and encourages the Republic of Cyprus to fully adopt the standards it contains.

records.section: Private security companies in the maritime context
records.text: 38. The use of private security companies in the maritime context has grown exponentially in response to the increase of threats of piracy, terrorism, attempted robberies and unlawful attacks against vessels in areas of the sea where there is considered to be high risk. This was particularly so between 2005 and 2009, when piracy incidents were occurring in the western Indian Ocean and the Gulf of Aden. Multiple strategies have been adopted by States to deal with those challenges and the expanding threats, including the deployment of naval counterpiracy operations and vessel protection detachments on ships flying their flag, the signing of the Jeddah Amendment to the Code of Conduct concerning the Repression of Piracy and Armed Robbery against Ships in the Western Indian Ocean and the Gulf of Aden, the application of industry standards and best practices of maritime securityand the adoption of legislation by flag States of vessels regulating the operation and hiring of armed and unarmed private military and security companies to protect vessels in high-risk areas. 39. Financial considerations play an important role in the use of private security companies. Many insurance companies require shipowners to pay exorbitant surcharges on premiums if their vessels pass through high-risk areas, or they refuse to insure the ships unless they have armed security personnel on board. Given the vast expanses of ocean involved, not to mention fiscal constraints, national navies are not well positioned to provide effective protection against unlawful acts. There is an increasing demand for cheaper services within the sector, resulting in greater competition, accompanied by a lowering of the quality of private security services at sea. Shipowners seek to provide the appearance of compliance with relevant standards and procedures by means of applications and certification, but without ensuring actual compliance at sea and the consequent negative impacts on human rights. Compounding these issues are the jurisdictional challenges and complexities of the high seas, where the isolated environment makes it difficult to investigate and enforce the law. 40. In the absence of clear and specific rules, in 2012, IMO developed interim guidance to private maritime security companies providing privately contracted armed security personnel on board ships in the high-risk area. The guidance provides that private security companies within the maritime sector should have verifiable, written internal policies and procedures for determining the suitability of persons to be deployed as privately contracted armed security personnel, including the checking of criminal records and employment history. Private maritime security companies should have a documented, robust and auditable health safety security environment policy with regard to incident investigation and a process for post-incident actions to support State authority investigations and prosecutions (should a formal investigation be required). They should ensure that personnel working for them have a complete understanding of, and fully comply with, the applicable laws governing the use of force. In particular, they should take all reasonable steps to avoid the use of force and, if force is used, it should be used as part of a graduated response plan and not exceed what is strictly necessary and reasonable in the circumstances. Care should be taken to minimize damage and injury and to respect and preserve human life. Since 2011, IMO has sought to systematically collect information from port States and coastal States on the relevant national legislation, policies and procedures relating to the deployment of maritime private security personnel and weapons use and storage. The Republic of Cyprus has yet to provide information pertaining to this. 41. In 2015, the International Organization for Standardization, with the support of IMO, published security management standard ISO 28007-1:2015 (previously ISO 28007:2012) on private maritime security companies providing privately contracted armed security personnel on board ships. Under the standard, such companies must hold valid accreditation certificates to demonstrate that they provide suitable privately contracted armed security personnel services on board ships. Certification under ISO 28007 is recognized by the International Code of Conduct for Private Security Service Providers’ Association as one way in which its member companies can demonstrate that their policies and procedures are in partial compliance with the International Code of Conduct for Private Security Service Providers. Additional governance and human rights documentation must be provided by a member company in order to obtain full certification by the Association, which is not without limitations as a regulatory mechanism. The Working Group is of the view that the maritime security industry requires a robust regulatory regime that is consistent with the rules for private security activities on land, and takes into account the specific context in which these companies operate. This has been echoed in numerous meetings held by the Working Group with private security companies within the maritime sector. 42. Although the use of private military and security companies contributes to more secure maritime transit, the Working Group has voiced concern about the impact that it can have on human rights, not least increased violence at sea and proliferation of weapons; disproportionate use of force; violations of the right to life, liberty and other physical integrity rights; torture; violations of due process guarantees; and abuses of labour rights. The domestic legal regimes of flag States play an important role in preventing human rights violations, including by ensuring that armed and unarmed security personnel hired and performing tasks are properly vetted and trained and that the rules for the use of force and the reporting of incidents at sea and how to achieve accountability and effective remedies for those affected in the event of human rights violations are clear.
